context: Al-Ahqaf is Makkan and comes last of the seven surahs that open with Ha Mim. Commentators place it late in the Makkan period, when the arguments had been made and refused and the pressure on the Prophet ﷺ was to hold a position rather than to win one. Its final instruction is to be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient.

Two things in it fit that setting. The passage on the jinn who stopped to listen and went home to their people as warners is commonly placed by the commentators on the return from Ta'if, when the Prophet ﷺ had been driven out of a town and had no human audience left, though reports differ over the details. And the destruction of 'Aad is told through their own mistake: they watched a cloud move toward their valleys and were pleased by it, because they took it for rain.
name_story: Al-Ahqaf is a place name, the long curving sand dunes where 'Aad lived, and it occurs once, in verse 21, where Hud is described warning his people there. The surah takes its title from a landscape rather than a doctrine or an argument. That fits what is left of 'Aad by the end of the account: dwellings standing in sand, with nothing else in view.

movements.note: Creation is stated to be in truth and for a fixed term. A challenge follows for those who call on others besides Allah: point to a piece of the earth they created, or produce a book from before this, or any remnant of transmitted knowledge.

movements.h: Not a novelty among the messengers
movements.note: The charge that the Qur'an was invented is met with the Prophet's ﷺ own limits: he is not the first of the messengers and does not know what will be done with him. A witness from the Children of Israel is mentioned, and those who say our Lord is Allah and then hold straight are told no fear will come upon them.

A man is enjoined to treat his parents well: his mother carried him with hardship, and thirty months cover his bearing and weaning. At forty he asks to be made grateful and to have his children set right. Beside him stands a son who says uff to his parents and denies he will ever be raised.

Hud warns his people and is told to bring on what he threatens. Seeing a cloud head for their valleys, they welcome it as rain. It is a wind, and afterwards nothing can be seen but their dwellings, though they had been given hearing, sight and hearts.

A company of jinn turns aside to hear the Qur'an, tells one another to keep quiet, and goes back to its people as warners. The surah closes on the power that made the heavens and the earth and on the order to endure as the resolute messengers endured.

themes.d: The demand in verse 4 is for a scripture or a remnant of knowledge, meaning a trace of something actually transmitted. A claim about God is treated as the kind of claim that has to come from somewhere and can be asked for.

Verse 9 has the Prophet ﷺ say that he does not know what will be done with him or with them. A claim to prophecy is kept separate here from a claim to independent knowledge of the unseen, and the surah keeps the two apart deliberately.

The du'a at forty is spoken by a man whose parents are now old and whose children are watching. Placing it next to the son who says uff shows the surah's interest: the same upbringing can produce either, and the difference surfaces in what each one says about being raised again.

'Aad saw the cloud and were pleased. The failure was not disbelief in that instant but a settled habit of reading whatever arrives as approval, which is also said of those who used up their good things in this life.

heart: Al-Ahqaf is a surah about correct hearing. A company of jinn catch a recitation by accident and immediately tell one another to be silent. 'Aad were given hearing and sight and hearts, and verse 26 states that none of it availed them anything. Between those two pictures the surah asks nothing of a reader except that he work out which one describes his own attention.

The verse most people take away is verse 15, and it repays being said slowly, because it holds a whole life in one sentence: hardship in carrying, hardship in delivery, thirty months, then forty years, then a request to be made grateful for what was spent on him and to have the same continue in his children. It is a du'a made by someone old enough to have added it up.

passages.why: The Prophet ﷺ is made to say that he is not the first of the messengers and does not know what will be done with him. A whole category of claims about him is ruled out here in his own words.
Those who say our Lord is Allah and then hold straight. A statement and a course of conduct, and the surah rests the entire promise of security on the pair of them together.

The verse on parents, the thirty months of bearing and weaning, and the du'a at forty. Jurists read it alongside the two years of nursing named in Al-Baqarah to derive a minimum term of pregnancy of six months.

The order to be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient. Commentators differ over who is meant, most naming a small group of the greatest messengers and some taking the phrase to include them all.

connections.why: Al-Jinn reports the same night from the other side and at greater length, in the listeners' own words. Al-Ahqaf keeps only what they did afterwards, which is the part its argument needs.
Al-Haqqah describes the end of 'Aad in detail, a wind loosed on them for seven nights and eight days. Al-Ahqaf gives the hour before that, while they were still watching the cloud and expecting rain.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Ahqaf. Its standing rests on its content, and on the fact that the episode in verses 29 to 32 is not an isolated tale: an account of the jinn hearing the Prophet's ﷺ recitation is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim on the authority of Ibn Abbas. That report establishes the event itself. It does not attach any reward to reciting the surah, and nothing authentic does.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; Ibn Abbas's account of the jinn in Bukhari and Muslim
